en: When he cried “Oh!” from his mouth
Blood poured in gush after gush.
While the Fierce One reeled,
That the Fierce One had slumped—
Your Syrgak saw as he rode.
“If I could seize him by the lowest hem,
And cut off his head!” he thought.
His two eyes became four with eagerness;
Like a blazing crimson fire,
Your Syrgak was dying with desire.
While the Fierce One swayed,
There was no wind striking his face.
As he turned back toward the Fierce One,
Almambet ahead of him
Over the cliff mentioned before
Was about to fall.
Then Syrgak arrived,
Paying no heed to the great Fierce One.
The moment your Syrgak reached him,
Of a swift steed like Sarala,
He gripped the bit firmly,
And from the top of the black cliff
He pulled him around and away.
He showed his lion's nature;
Your Almam, big as a hut,
He gripped firmly by the shoulder-blades,
And set him upon the white saddle.
He kindled his extinguished fire.
In this way, hero Syrgak
Your Almam's deadened life
Revived through his valor.
With life poised between death and survival,
Kongurbay writhed.
Striking his own head,
Kongurbay wept:
“From atop the black cliff,
As I was about to thrust him over,
Of Sarala and the fugitive,
As I was about to cut off their heads,
God was to strike me down!
Kökchebich beneath him—
No beast can catch him by running.
Syrgak riding upon him—
No strength can overcome him in combat.
Syrgak has everything in his favor.
Except that Manas possesses sacred might,
Manas's hero Syrgak
Is a man to match him at lancing.
His skill is extraordinary;
It went through my every bone,
The lance he thrust into my flank.
Had Syrgak not been here,
Would I not have split his heart?
Would I not have brought upon his head
A disaster no one had ever seen?
Would I not have broken his might?
If I killed Almambet,
Would I not receive from the great khan
The khanly rule I asked for?”
Saying these words then,
Kongurbay, wounded,
Was filled with fury.
To his seething multitude
He turned and went back.
When Kongurbay arrived,
All the Chinese gathered,
Every renowned warrior,
Not sparing his own life,
Prepared to sweep over them.
All the champions,
Forming ranks of troops,
With earth flying up as dust,
Covered in dust and turned gray,
Made the ground sway with their swarming.
Beijing's golden banner with its black crescent
They put into the lama's hands.
So that the Chinese would not flee back,
If you looked behind the army,
Skilled horseman and swift foot-runner,
Giant Mangkush was made to drive them on.
That they would fight face to face,
They all knew as they came.
Behind them, iron-eared giant Kutan
Came driving them forward.
All the Chinese prepared,
Heading toward a single place,
Massed against Almambet;
Among the Chinese of the dark faith,
An upheaval had arisen.
The Fierce One turned, that formidable man,
That accursed leopard hero,
Before the multitude of infidels
Came out for single combat.
Noticing this, Almambet
Turned his horse's head.
Offering his thoughts to Syrgak,
He stood consulting with him.
“My Syrgak,
My horses in the mountains number nine thousand,
A mixture of fine-bred horses and winged steeds.
Fine-bred horses and winged steeds, well fed—
If I die at that hell-dweller's hands,
To cry out ‘My Almambet!’ after me,
I have no child to follow in my tracks.
What God has ordained,
There is no way but to bear it!
Sarala, my winged steed, is my companion.
If I die here,
Where might a lone, desolate head not be left?
My leopard, my Syrgak,
Since I came to the Muslims,
My burden has been one.
Aruuke, daughter of Agynay—
It has been years since I married her.
She does not spread her hair and comb it;
Her heels do not bleed.
Childless, our days have turned black.
If I happen to die at Chinese hands,
As though your companion Almam were still here,
Do not begin a battle with the enemy.
What I entrust to you is this:
Do not leave my bones with the Chinese!
Bend me at the waist and fold me,
Onto my life's companion, though a beast,
Onto Sarala, load me and go.
If you come upon a burial place,
Dig my grave wide;
Recite the Quran in my name,
Slaughter Sarala,
Dig deep and lay me there!
Keep driving your countless horses.
Let me die if my doom has come;
Those Chinese who boast of bravery—
Let me stand before them here
And see how able they are.”
As though a lance had pierced him,
Hero Syrgak sprang up:
“Perish with your horses!
My joy, my Almam, I shall not drive them!
By driving the horses away,
What desire would I fulfill?
My precious Almam, my lion,
Leaving him alone among the Chinese—
How could I abandon him and go?
If my doom has come, I shall die.
Kongurbay, son of Alöökö—
Ah, world, I have been left yearning!
I shall face him once and see!
Leave me here, dear Almambet;
Look after your horses yourself.
Me, your younger brother Syrgak,
Expect me within seven days!”
Clasping hands and saying farewell,
The two lions, not moving away,
Held each other's hands.
Without saying many other things,
Entrusting their final charges,
Hero Almambet, your pale goshawk,
Behind those countless myriads of horses
Your dear fellow rode.
He drove the horses onward,
Crashing upon the war drum,
Blasting with his lacquered musket,
Making them clatter and thunder.
Almambet herded them together:
The dense myriads of horses
He set surging ahead of him,
And drove them hard, your Almambet.
Let Almambet, driving the horses,
Continue on his way.
Let us leave him there
And turn to the single combat behind him,
Beginning with the warrior Syrgak.
“Kongurbay has come out to single combat;
Let me die in a skirmish with him.
At least, if we meet,
Let me die fighting face to face.
Taking careful aim at the fierce one,
Let me strike him with my spear.
If the Chinese warrior comes close,
Let me seize him by his forelock.
This time, upon the fierce one,
Let me lay a special grief,” he thought.
He turned Kokchebich’s head,
Your wolf-man, valiant Syrgak.
“When will Kongurbay come?” he said.
He appeared upon a grassy rise,
And stood looking back.
Among the Chinese of Beijing
A khan named Alooko had arisen.
When Alooko’s Kongurbay
Roared, those who heard him
Had their souls driven out by his voice.
“Where is the Kyrgyz, where?” he cried.
“Seize him and bind his hands!”
He had worked himself into a rage.
Looking at the fierce one,
He was truly a giant among mighty men;
Of the Chinese people’s forty khans,
He was indeed the master.
When one looked at his bearing,
He loomed like a towering mountain.
The myriad troops behind him
Were divided into many bands.
But for his unbelief,
His countenance was open and favorable.
The unbelievers’ Kongurbay
Was so much larger than other men.
A single hair of his moustache
Was like a battle-axe’s haft.
His nose was like a mountain spur;
He seemed ready to eat any who struggled.
His eyes were like secluded lake inlets;
He seemed ready to swallow anyone he saw.
The corners of his two eyes
Were like graves left open.
The breadth of his moonlike forehead
Was like the upper summer pasture.
Taking no account of his surroundings,
Sparing his life in no way,
He did not turn and look back.
Look at his valor!
He did not spare his threadlike life.
His finely wrought spear of sharp steel
He thrust out with a shout.
His ravenous steel sword, Beijing’s scourge,
He laid upon his bare wrist.
His matchlock for shooting,
That too he readied,
Kongurbay had taken it up.
Black was his felt cap’s brim;
With no concern for brow or eyebrows,
He watched, licking his lips:
Khan Manas’s Syrgak.
Plain-spoken in this world,
Clear-sighted among humankind,
Alooko’s Kongurbay,
From the moment he saw Syrgak,
Came judging him, the fierce one:
“Kokchebich beneath him—
No beast can match him when urged on.
As for Syrgak upon his back,
No strength can overcome him in a grapple.
He will jolt me wide awake;
He will devastate my people,
Chasing them in helpless flight,
Making rivers of blood flow.
He will slaughter my people,
He will break my back;
Smashing everything to pieces,
He will plunder my land.
Syrgak is indeed a warrior;
He is favored in every way.
His right shoulder is broad.
But for his being Kyrgyz,
He is a lion in this fleeting world.
